✅ Quick check: Tenses

1. Fill in: "By the time we arrived, the guests ___ (leave)."

had left. It's the earlier past action, so use the past perfect.

2. Fill in: "Listen! Someone ___ (knock) at the door."

is knocking (present continuous; "Listen!" = happening now).

3. Correct: "I have seen that film last week."

I saw that film last week (finished time → past simple).

4. Fill in: "She ___ (learn) French for three years and is still learning."

has been learning (present perfect continuous).

📽️ Revision slideshow: Determiners

1. What is a determiner?

A determiner is a word that comes before a noun (and before any adjectives) to tell us which one, how many / how much, or whose. It "determines" the noun.

Pattern: determiner + (adjective) + noun → those tall trees • a big red bus • my new phone • many happy children

Tip: the determiner always goes first. ❌ red a bus → ✅ a red bus.

2. Articles: a, an, the

ArticleUseExample
a
indefinite		One singular countable thing, not a specific one / mentioned for the first time. Before a consonant sound.a dog, a book, a university, a uniform, a one-way street
an
indefinite		Same as "a", but before a vowel sound.an apple, an egg, an hour, an honest girl, an MP3 player
the
definite		A specific thing both people know about; something mentioned before; the only one.I saw a cat. The cat was black. • the sun, the moon
It's the SOUND, not the letter! "hour" starts with a silent h → sounds like "our" → an hour. "university" sounds like "you-niversity" → a university.

Use "the" with…

  • Things there is only one of: the sun, the sky, the internet
  • Superlatives and ordinals: the tallest building, the first chapter
  • Rivers, seas, oceans, deserts, mountain ranges: the Ganga, the Arabian Sea, the Thar Desert, the Himalayas
  • Musical instruments: She plays the piano / the harmonica.
  • Countries with "states / kingdom / republic" or plural names: the UAE, the USA, the Netherlands

Use NO article (zero article) with…

  • Names of people, most countries, cities, single mountains: Sara, India, Dubai, Mount Everest
  • Languages and school subjects: She speaks French. I like maths.
  • Sports and meals: We play cricket. We have lunch at one.
  • Plural or uncountable nouns used in general: Dogs are loyal. Water is important.

3. Demonstratives: this, that, these, those

Demonstratives point to something. They show near or far and singular or plural.

Singular (one)Plural (more than one)
Near (here)this bookthese books
Far (there)that bookthose books
Time works too: this week (now) • that day (in the past) • these days (nowadays) • in those days (long ago)

Determiner or pronoun? If a noun follows, it's a determiner: "This bag is heavy." If it stands alone, it's a pronoun: "This is heavy."

4. Quantifiers: how many? how much?

Quantifiers tell us the amount. Which one you use depends on whether the noun is countable (you can count it: apples, books, friends) or uncountable (you can't count it: water, sugar, money, homework, advice, information, furniture).

Only countable (plural)Only uncountableBoth
many books
a few friends
few people
several times
a number of students		much water
a little sugar
little time
a great deal of money
a bit of help		some, any, no
a lot of / lots of
plenty of, enough
all, most, more

some or any?

WordUseExample
somePositive sentences; offers and requestsI bought some bread. Would you like some tea? Can I have some water?
anyNegative sentences and most questionsWe don't have any milk. Is there any juice left?

few vs a few • little vs a little

WordMeaningFeelingExample
a few (countable)some, a small number😊 positive: enoughI have a few friends here, so I'm not lonely.
few (countable)almost none😟 negative: not enoughFew students finished the test. It was very hard.
a little (uncountable)some, a small amount😊 positiveThere's a little time left, let's check our answers.
little (uncountable)almost none😟 negativeWe have little water left. We must find more.

each, every, either, neither, both

  • each / every + singular noun + singular verb: Every student has a locker. Each player gets a medal.
  • each = one by one (often 2 or more); every = all of a group (3 or more).
  • either / neither + singular noun (choice of two): You can sit in either chair. Neither answer is correct.
  • both + plural noun (two together): Both teams played well.

5. Possessive determiners: whose?

PersonPossessive determinerExample
Imymy bag
youyouryour book
hehishis bike
sheherher phone
ititsThe cat licked its paw.
weourour school
theytheirtheir house
Watch out! its (belongs to it) ≠ it's (it is). their (belongs to them) ≠ there (place) ≠ they're (they are). your ≠ you're (you are).

Possessive determiners come before a noun (my pen). Possessive pronouns stand alone (The pen is mine).

6. Using more than one determiner

Some determiners can go together, in this order:

1st: all / both / half2nd: the / this / my…3rd: numbers / first / last / few / manyNoun
allmyfriends
boththegirls
thefirst twochapters
halftheclass
thesethreebooks

❌ my all friends → ✅ all my friends • ❌ the my book → ✅ my book (never use two from column 2).

7. Common mistakes

❌ Wrong✅ RightWhy
I waited for a hour.I waited for an hour."hour" starts with a vowel sound (silent h).
She is an university student.She is a university student."university" starts with a "y" sound.
How many money do you have?How much money do you have?Money is uncountable → much.
I need some informations.I need some information.Uncountable nouns have no plural.
Every students have a book.Every student has a book.every + singular noun + singular verb.
This shoes are new.These shoes are new.Plural noun → these/those.
The dog wagged it's tail.The dog wagged its tail.it's = it is.
I don't have some money.I don't have any money.Negative → any.
Sun rises in east.The sun rises in the east.Only one sun; directions take "the".
She plays the cricket.She plays cricket.No article with sports.

✅ Quick check: Determiners

1. Fill in a, an or the: "She is ___ honest girl."

an (honest has a silent h, so it starts with a vowel sound).

2. Choose: "How (much / many) homework do you have?"

much (homework is uncountable).

3. Correct: "Look at that birds in the sky."

Look at those birds in the sky (plural + far).

4. What's the difference? "Few people came." / "A few people came."

"Few" = almost nobody came (negative). "A few" = some people came (positive).

5. Fill in: "The tree lost ___ leaves in winter." (its / it's)

its (belonging to the tree). "It's" means "it is".

📽️ Revision slideshow: Dialogue Writing

1. What good dialogue does

Dialogue is a conversation between characters. In good writing it is never just "filler". Every line should do at least one job:

  • Reveal character: how someone speaks shows who they are (polite, rude, nervous, bossy, funny).
  • Move the plot forward: give information, make a decision, create a problem.
  • Create conflict or tension: disagreement makes readers want to know what happens.
  • Show relationships: friends tease, strangers are formal, a parent and child speak differently.
Show, don't tell: Instead of "Ravi was angry", write: "Don't touch my things," Ravi snapped, slamming the drawer shut.

2. Punctuation rules (story format)

  • Use a new paragraph every time the speaker changes.
  • Don't overuse "said". Choose verbs that show how something is said: whispered, shouted, muttered, insisted, laughed, sighed, admitted, demanded, pleaded. But "said" is fine sometimes. Don't make every line dramatic.
  • Add actions (beats) between lines: She folded her arms. "Fine."
  • Keep speech natural: short sentences, contractions (I'm, don't), and interruptions shown with a dash (—) or trailing off (…).

3. Script (play) format

If the question asks for a dialogue in script form, use no speech marks. Write the speaker's name, a colon, then the words. Stage directions go in brackets and italics.

Setting: A school corridor after the science fair results are announced.

Zaid: (waving the results sheet) We came fourth. Fourth! I told you the volcano was a bad idea.
Aisha: The volcano worked. It was the explanation that was weak.
Zaid: Because you wrote it in five minutes!
Aisha: (quietly) Because you spent three days painting the volcano.
Zaid: (pauses) …Okay. That's fair. Next time I'll do the research and you do the model?
Aisha: (smiling) Deal. But I'm choosing the colour.

Why this works: each speaker has a clear attitude (Zaid is dramatic and blaming; Aisha is calm and honest), there is conflict, the problem is solved, and the last line ends with a touch of humour.

4. Exam checklist for dialogue

  1. Does it suit the situation and the characters (formal or informal)?
  2. Does it have a beginning (greeting/situation), a middle (problem/discussion) and an end (decision/closing)?
  3. Does each speaker have a distinct voice?
  4. Are punctuation and new lines correct?
  5. Did you stay within the word/line limit?
📽️ Revision slideshow: Travelogue

1. What is a travelogue?

A travelogue is a piece of writing about a journey or a place someone has visited. It mixes information (where, when, what you saw) with personal experience (what you felt, learnt and remember). It should make the reader feel they travelled with you.

Features

  • Written in the first person ("I", "we"), usually in the past tense.
  • Chronological order (the journey in sequence) with time connectives: at dawn, by noon, later that evening.
  • Vivid sensory details: sights, sounds, smells, tastes, textures.
  • Facts about the place: history, food, culture, people.
  • Figurative language: similes, metaphors, personification.
  • Reflection: what the trip meant to you or what you learnt.

2. Structure

PartWhat to write
TitleCatchy and specific: "Golden Dunes and Silver Stars: Two Days in Jaisalmer"
Introduction (hook)Start in the middle of a moment, with a sound, an image or a question. Say where you went and why.
Body paragraphsOne paragraph per place or part of the day. Describe with the senses, include a fact, and say how you felt.
ConclusionReflect: what stayed with you, what you learnt, whether you would return.

3. Model travelogue

A Morning in Old Dubai

The abra's engine coughed twice, then settled into a steady putter as we pulled away from the Bur Dubai side of the Creek. Spray flicked across my arm, cool for a moment against the already-warm air. It cost just one dirham to cross, yet the water taxi felt like a doorway into another century.

On the Deira side, the Spice Souk swallowed us whole. Sacks of turmeric glowed like little suns, and dried limes, black and wrinkled, rattled when the shopkeeper scooped them. The air was thick with cinnamon and cardamom, so rich I could almost taste it. "Smell this," the trader said, pressing a pinch of saffron into my palm. "From Iran. The best." I believed him.

The Gold Souk next door was quieter but dazzling. Window after window blazed with bangles and necklaces, as if someone had melted the sun and poured it into shapes. My younger brother pressed his nose to the glass until Mum gently pulled him away.

By eleven, the heat had become a heavy blanket, so we retreated to Al Fahidi, where narrow lanes are shaded by tall wind towers called barjeel. Before air conditioning, these towers caught passing breezes and pushed them down into the houses. Standing beneath one, I felt a faint, surprising coolness and marvelled at how clever people had been without any electricity.

As the abra carried us back, the glass towers of modern Dubai shimmered on the horizon. I realised the city I thought I knew had an older heart, one that smelled of spices and moved at the speed of a wooden boat.

Why it scores well: opens in action with sound (onomatopoeia "putter"); every paragraph uses senses; includes facts (one dirham, barjeel wind towers); similes ("glowed like little suns"); dialogue for life; time connectives (By eleven, As the abra…); a reflective ending that links back to the start.

4. Upgrades

WeakStrong
The market was busy and nice.Traders shouted prices over the clatter of carts while the scent of fried samosas drifted between the stalls.
The sea was blue.The sea stretched out like a sheet of crumpled turquoise silk.
It was very hot.The heat pressed down on my shoulders, and even the shadows seemed to sweat.
We went to many places. It was fun.By sunset we had climbed a fort, bargained for bangles and eaten our weight in kachoris, and I didn't want the day to end.
📽️ Revision slideshow: V.O.I.C.E. & P.A.W.S. (your class version)

V.O.I.C.E.: understanding a character

LetterAsk yourselfUseful sentence starters
V – VoiceWho is telling the story? How do they speak (first person "I", calm, excited, scared)?"The story is told by…", "Vega's voice is…"
O – OpinionsWhat does the character believe or think about others and the world? And what is your opinion?"Vega believes that…", "In my opinion…"
I – InterestsWhat do they want, love or care about most?"More than anything, Deneb wants…"
C – ConcernsWhat worries, fears or problems do they have?"Vega is worried that…", "Jesse fears…"
E – ExperiencesWhat happens to them, and how does it change them?"After…, Vega learns…", "This experience changes Jesse because…"

P.A.W.S.: understanding the story as a whole

LetterAsk yourselfUseful sentence starters
P – PowerWho has power and who doesn't? Does power shift during the story?"At first the humans have power over…, but…"
A – AtmosphereWhat is the mood of a scene (tense, peaceful, sad, frightening)? Which details create it?"The atmosphere is… because the writer describes…"
W – Writer's perspectiveWhat does the author (or film-maker) believe? What message do they want us to take away?"The writer wants readers to realise that…"
S – SymbolismWhich objects, places or actions stand for a bigger idea?"The salmon symbolise…", "Willy's leap represents…"
📽️ Revision slideshow: A Whale of the Wild & Free Willy

🎯 The exam question

The last question gives you a choice: A Whale of the Wild OR Free Willy. It is an analysis question about a theme, a character or a relationship, not "retell the story". You answer in a long note: 4 paragraphs (Introduction, Details, Opinion, Conclusion) in 100–120 words. Questions focus on Chapters 8–15, but earlier chapters could come up.

The kinds of questions you'll get

Question typeExampleWhat the examiner wants
Theme"Explain how the idea of courage is presented in Chapters 8–15."Where the theme appears, with 2–3 moments as evidence, and what the writer is saying about it
Compare"Compare the different ways Vega and Deneb demonstrate bravery."One way for EACH character, with a moment each, plus how they are different (and alike)
Relationship"Explain how Deneb and the stranger orca (the Seal-eater) develop an unexpected connection."How it starts → how it grows → why it is surprising
"What does it suggest…?""What does this relationship suggest about helping others despite differences?"The message / lesson: put it in your Conclusion, and hint at it in the Opinion
Character change"How does Vega's attitude towards humans change?"Before → turning point → after

How to fit an analysis question into the 4 paragraphs

ParagraphWhat to writeStarters
1 Introduction (≈20–25 words)Name the book/author or the film. Answer the question in one sentence using its key words."In Chapters 8–15 of A Whale of the Wild, Rosanne Parry presents courage as…"
2 Details (≈40–50 words)2–3 specific moments from the chapters as evidence. For "compare", one for each character, joined by whereas / however / on the other hand."For example…", "In Chapter 10…", "Later, during the sea shake…", "However, Deneb…"
3 Opinion (≈15–25 words)Your view with a reason. For a comparison, say whose bravery you think is greater and why."I think… because…", "In my opinion…", "I admire… because…"
4 Conclusion (≈12–18 words)The big message. This is where you answer "What does it suggest…?""This suggests that…", "Overall, Parry shows that…"
Top tips: Use the question's own words in your first and last sentence (courage, bravery, unexpected connection, despite differences). Don't retell the whole plot: choose only the events that prove your point. Always explain why an event shows the idea, e.g. "…which shows his kindness is stronger than his fear."

🐋 A Whale of the Wild – Rosanne Parry (2020)

What it's about: Vega is a young orca (killer whale) in the Salish Sea (the waters between Washington state, USA, and British Columbia, Canada). She is training to become her family's wayfinder, the one who remembers the routes and leads the pod to food. The salmon her family eats are disappearing. After her baby sister dies and a huge sea shake (earthquake and tsunami) changes the sea forever, Vega and her little brother Deneb are separated from their family and must survive on their own.

How it's told: In the first person, switching between Vega and Deneb as narrators. Orcas have their own words: sea shake = earthquake/tsunami, Blue Wilderness = the open ocean, longboats = canoes of Indigenous people, Seal-eaters = a different orca group that hunts seals instead of salmon. The story echoes real events: in 2018 a real Southern Resident orca, Tahlequah, carried her dead calf for 17 days.

Characters

CharacterWho they are
VegaMain narrator. A young orca learning to be a wayfinder. Named after a bright star. Feels guilt, grief and anger, but grows into a brave, caring leader.
DenebVega's little brother and second narrator. Chatty, loyal, wants to be a hero like Uncle Rigel. Brave but impulsive.
GreatmotherThe wise elder and wayfinder of the pod. Her sayings guide Vega: "Eat a little beauty every day… it will give you strength" and "When the sea shakes, the ocean is a refuge."
MotherVega and Deneb's mother. Gives birth to Capella, who does not survive.
CapellaVega's baby sister, who dies at birth (Chapter 6).
Uncle RigelA heroic uncle who saved Mother at Blood Cove long ago. Deneb looks up to him.
Aquila & AltairVega's cousin and her baby son.
The Seal-eaterA big orca from a different kinship that eats seals. Deneb helps free him from a trap line.
The longboat ridersIndigenous people who respect the sea. In Greatmother's stories, whales and longboat people once lived in peace.
The Vanished OnesA long-lost branch of orcas who live in the open ocean and hunt sharks (later chapters).

Chapters 1–7 (background – know these too!)

ChapterWhat happensWhy it matters
1 – Kinship
(Vega)		It is early morning in the misty Salish Sea. Vega's family has hunted all night without finding salmon, and everyone is tired and hungry. Vega is no longer a youngling, but she isn't yet strong enough to hunt like Mother or wise enough to be a wayfinder like Greatmother, and she worries she will never be good enough. She dances in the mist to cheer herself up. Greatmother tells her, "Eat a little beauty every day, my Vega, my bright star… it will give you strength." Vega doesn't understand, because she is so hungry. Mother is pregnant with Capella, so food matters even more. After a long, frustrating day Vega catches only a small flatfish, which the family shares. Later she catches a salmon. She is tempted to keep it for herself, but when she hears her family calling she shares it.Introduces the family, the hunger caused by disappearing salmon, Vega's self-doubt and her selfless nature. The "beauty" saying comes back later.
2 – NoiseMother and Greatmother praise Vega's catch and decide she should start learning to lead as a wayfinder. Her cousin Aquila often interrupts and outshines her, which annoys Vega. On the way to the Gathering Place, Vega leads the family through familiar waters, but they meet the deafening roar of a huge human ship. Vega insists they keep going, and she nearly leads the pod into its path. The noise causes panic, and the older whales guide everyone to safety in a kelp forest. Mother reminds her that you learn to lead by trying. Ashamed, Vega swims off alone.Vega's first big mistake as a leader. Shows the danger of ship noise and traffic to orcas.
3 – BirdsFull of guilt, Vega believes her family would be better off without her. She hunts alone and passes seals, octopuses and fish. She watches murres and puffins diving skilfully and even envies a plain minke whale that eats well. Desperately hungry, she catches a gull, but orcas of her family don't eat birds. Aquila finds her and scolds her for forgetting the family's ways. Then Aquila softens, encourages her, and persuades her to come back and search for salmon together. The cousins swim side by side.Shows Vega's guilt and loneliness and the importance of family rules and values. Aquila turns from rival to support.
4 – GatheringVega and Aquila look for the family. Vega's calls go unanswered, and she remembers younglings who were lost before. Aquila is excited to be first to find the returning Chinook salmon, whose yearly return feeds the whole kinship. Near a human gathering, an earth tremor shakes the water. Aquila tells a story about the earth shaking to calm her, but Vega stays uneasy. They find Deneb and the rest of the family, including little cousin Altair, and celebrate the salmon's return. Vega realises that caring for her family matters more than being first or fastest.The small tremor foreshadows the great sea shake later. The salmon run links to the theme of survival.
5 – Long DanceThe whole kinship meets for the Gathering, a summer reunion with dancing, games and storytelling. Orcas call out their names as they leap and spin in the Long Dance. Dolphins hunt nearby while others rest in a "sleep line". Late at night, Greatmother tells Vega and Aquila about a tremor long ago that reshaped the sea. She teaches that if the earth shakes again, the open ocean is a refuge, and that together is better than apart. Deneb, pretending to sleep, has been listening, and he promises Vega, "I will always follow you."Joyful atmosphere before tragedy. Greatmother's teaching later saves Vega (Ch 13). Deneb's promise sets up Chapter 9, "Follow".
6 – Birth
(Deneb)		On the first night of the Gathering, Mother goes into labour. The wayfinders and great hunters circle her while the uncles stand guard. The blood draws sharks, and Deneb proudly helps Uncle Rigel and the other uncles drive them away. Greatmother lifts the newborn, a "tiny black and golden-pink sister", to the surface. Deneb feels relief and joy, but Capella cannot breathe. Mother had lost a baby before, too. Uncle Rigel comforts the family: "I am here… I am beside you." Deneb copies him by nuzzling Vega. The mothers sing a lament, "high-pitched and fierce and full of longing".Huge turning point: grief. Shows Deneb's wish to be a protector like Uncle Rigel.
7 – Stolen
(Vega)		Vega grieves for Capella, who was meant to share her hunting and wayfinding. Greatmother tells Mother the death is not her fault. She blames poisons and changes in the sea, because many babies have been lost. When Greatmother says it's time to let Capella go, Vega is filled with rage at the thought of her sister lying in a cold passage with boats roaring overhead. She takes Capella's body on her back and races away towards Deception Pass. She tells Capella the story of Blood Cove: when Mother was a baby, three boats and a helicopter chased the pod. The mothers lured the boats away, and Uncle Rigel saved Mother and Aunt Nova, but the other uncles were killed and the babies were captured. Vega promises, "I will lay you beside the bones of the uncles who saved your mother."Shows Vega's love and anger at humans, and explains the history behind Chapter 8.

⭐ Chapters 8–15 (exam focus)

ChapterNarratorWhat happensWhy it matters
8 – Blood CoveVegaVega remembers wanting revenge on humans after hearing about Blood Cove. But she once saw human parents sharing food with their children, and now a pregnant woman with a small child watches her silently from the shore. Vega wonders if human poisons hurt human babies too. She lays Capella beside the bones of the uncles and decides to carry her sadness and help her family.Turning point: anger → compassion. Shows grief and the human impact on the sea.
9 – FollowDenebDeneb is torn between guarding Mother and following Vega. Uncle Rigel tells him wayfinders follow their hearts and memories, and a brother's job is to trust them. He asks Deneb to bring Vega home. Deneb has never travelled alone but bravely sets off, heading for Tree Island, where Vega taught him to catch salmon.Deneb starts to grow up. Theme of family loyalty.
10 – RescueDenebAt Tree Island, Deneb finds a huge Seal-eater orca tangled in a crab-trap line, barely able to breathe. Greatmother warned him to avoid Seal-eaters, but he can't leave a trapped whale. Two humans in an orange boat arrive. Deneb splashes them and nudges their boat, and they cut the line and leave. The freed orca whistles thanks.Deneb is a hero in his own way. Irony: the humans were actually helping, but Deneb thinks he scared them off.
11 – LongboatsVegaLonely after Blood Cove, Vega meets the quiet longboats and greets their riders as family, as Greatmother taught, and they greet her back. Entering Deception Pass under a bridge, she glimpses Deneb and a large whale on the other side. Then the sea shakes and part of the bridge collapses, blocking the passage.Hope (peace between humans and whales) suddenly broken by disaster.
12 – Sea ShakeDenebThe sea shake churns the water, and boulders crash down. The Seal-eater urges Deneb to swim for deep water, and porpoises rush by with the same warning. Deneb is surprised he understands them. Cars ("land boats") fall from the bridge and seal off Deception Pass. Deneb worries how he'll ever find Vega.Frightening, chaotic atmosphere. Different creatures unite in danger.
13 – Deception PassVegaVega hears Deneb calling and cries out to him through the chaos. Porpoises hurrying past remind her of Greatmother's teaching, "When the sea shakes, the ocean is a refuge." She calms herself and navigates towards the ocean from memory.Vega uses memory and calm, the skills of a wayfinder.
14 – WavesVegaA strong current ("the Pull") sweeps Vega along. She meets a mother whale and calf and joins their chant. She finds Deneb and the Seal-eater. When a giant wave rises, Vega tells them to dive, and they survive. Afterwards they see overturned boats and struggling people. By sunset Vega accepts that home has changed and moves on.Vega acts as a true leader and saves lives.
15 – Land's EndVegaAt dawn they reach the last island before the open ocean, the edge of the Blue Wilderness that Greatmother warned them never to enter. Their family is not there. Vega feels guilty for leaving them at their darkest time and responsible for Deneb. Deneb wants to go back to the Salish Sea, but Vega refuses because the water is now poisoned and dangerous.Big decision; Vega takes on responsibility for her brother.

After Chapter 15 (so you know the ending)

Ch 16 "Seal": the Seal-eater shares a seal and Deneb gets sick; Vega explains each creature should eat its own food to keep the sea in balance. Ch 17 "Lost": the changed coastline, little food. Ch 18 "Blue Wilderness": they bravely enter the open ocean and see a giant whale. Ch 19–20: they meet the Vanished Ones; during a shark hunt Deneb is injured protecting Vega, and she cares for him. Ch 21–25: they return home, find only Aquila and Altair (thin and hungry), Vega guides them to salmon, helps the longboat people clear a river mouth blocked by rubble so the salmon can swim upstream, and becomes the pod's wayfinder, ready to lead them to food and family.

V.O.I.C.E. – Vega and Deneb

VegaDeneb
VoiceFirst person, thoughtful, emotional, uses orca words (sea shake, Blue Wilderness)First person, younger, chatty, eager, sometimes funny
OpinionsAt first she thinks all humans are cruel; after Blood Cove she sees humans have families tooBelieves in being a hero like Uncle Rigel; trusts his sister completely
InterestsBecoming a good wayfinder; feeding and protecting her familyFinding Vega; rescuing others; making his family proud
ConcernsHunger, the disappearing salmon, failing her family, guilt over leaving them, poisons in the waterGetting lost alone, losing Vega, being too young
ExperiencesLoses Capella, survives the sea shake, leads Deneb through danger → becomes a leaderTravels alone, frees the Seal-eater, survives the sea shake → grows braver and more independent

P.A.W.S. – A Whale of the Wild

PowerHumans have huge power over the orcas: ships, noise, fishing lines, poisons, and the captures at Blood Cove. Nature has power too (the sea shake). The orcas gain power through knowledge and leadership: Vega's wayfinding, Greatmother's wisdom.
AtmospherePeaceful and joyful at the Gathering; deeply sad in Chapters 6–8 (Capella's death, Blood Cove); terrifying and chaotic in Chapters 11–14 (boulders, collapsing bridge, giant wave); lonely and uncertain at Land's End.
Writer's perspectiveParry tells the story through orca eyes so readers care about real Southern Resident orcas. She wants us to see how overfishing, pollution and ship noise harm them, and that humans and animals can live in peace (the longboat riders).
SymbolismSalmon = survival and the health of the sea. Vega's star = hope and guidance. Blood Cove = past human cruelty and grief. The Blue Wilderness = fear of the unknown, and courage. The longboats = peace and respect between humans and nature. The sea shake = sudden change nobody can control.

🎬 Free Willy (1993 film, directed by Simon Wincer)

What it's about: Jesse is a 12-year-old boy whose mother abandoned him. He lives on the streets of Portland, Oregon. Willy is a young orca captured from his family and kept in a small tank at an adventure park. Two lonely characters form a friendship, and Jesse risks everything to set Willy free.

Characters

CharacterWho they are
JesseTough, angry runaway who trusts no one. He changes into a caring, responsible boy.
WillyThe captured orca. Lonely and aggressive at first, he bonds only with Jesse.
Glen & Annie GreenwoodJesse's patient foster parents. They help free Willy at the end.
Rae LindleyWilly's animal trainer, who cares about him.
Randolph JohnsonThe park's caretaker, a Haida man who tells Jesse orca legends and becomes his mentor.
DialThe greedy park owner who sees Willy only as money.
WadeDial's assistant, who damages Willy's tank.
DwightJesse's social worker.

The story in scenes

  1. Capture: Willy is netted in the ocean and separated from his family.
  2. Caught: Jesse and his friends vandalise the adventure park with graffiti. Jesse is caught. Instead of juvenile detention, he goes to live with foster parents Glen and Annie, and must clean the graffiti.
  3. Meeting Willy: While cleaning, Jesse meets Willy, who scares everyone else. When Jesse slips into the tank, Willy saves him. Jesse's harmonica music calms Willy.
  4. Friendship and training: Rae and Randolph see the special bond. Jesse trains Willy to do tricks, and Jesse starts to trust adults and open up to the Greenwoods.
  5. The failed show: On show day the noisy crowd bangs on the glass. Willy panics and won't perform. Dial is furious.
  6. The plot: Jesse discovers Dial's men damaging the tank so Willy will die and Dial can collect insurance money.
  7. The escape: Jesse, Rae and Randolph move Willy into a trailer at night. Glen and Annie join to help. Dial's men block the harbour.
  8. The leap: Jesse leads Willy to the rock jetty and Willy makes an enormous jump over it to freedom. He swims away to rejoin his family. Jesse accepts the Greenwoods as his own family.

V.O.I.C.E. – Jesse

VoiceRude, defensive and short-tempered at first ("I don't need anyone"); later gentle, especially when talking to Willy
OpinionsBelieves adults always let you down; later learns to trust Glen, Annie, Rae and Randolph
InterestsFinding his mother, freedom; then Willy's happiness and safety
ConcernsBeing abandoned again, being sent away; that Willy will die in the tank
ExperiencesLiving on the street, getting caught, bonding with Willy, saving him → he learns love, trust and responsibility

P.A.W.S. – Free Willy

PowerDial has money and power over Willy (and the adults). Jesse seems powerless, but friendship and courage give him the power to free Willy. Power shifts from the greedy owner to the boy and his friends.
AtmosphereGloomy and tense at the start (streets, the small grey tank); warm and joyful in the training scenes; frightening at the show; thrilling and suspenseful during the night escape; triumphant at the final jump.
Writer's perspectiveThe film-makers believe wild animals like orcas should not be kept in captivity for entertainment, and that every child deserves love and a family.
SymbolismThe tank = captivity and loneliness. The harmonica = the bond between Jesse and Willy. The jetty leap = freedom and new beginnings. Willy's family = the family Jesse longs for.

Comparing the two

A Whale of the WildFree Willy
Point of viewTold by orcas (Vega, Deneb)Mainly a human's story (Jesse)
Main problemHunger, pollution, the sea shake, finding familyCaptivity, a greedy owner, a lonely boy
Humans shown asBoth harmful (poisons, Blood Cove) and kind (longboat riders, the pregnant woman)Both greedy (Dial, Wade) and caring (Jesse, Rae, Randolph, the Greenwoods)
Shared themesFamily and belonging • courage • humans' effect on wildlife • the bond between people and orcas • growing up

📝 Model long notes (all 100–120 words)

These answer the kinds of questions you'll actually get. Notice how each one uses the question's words in the first and last paragraph.

💡 Ideas bank: themes in Chapters 8–15

ThemeEvidence (chapter)
Courage / braveryVega faces grief at Blood Cove (8) • Deneb travels alone for the first time (9) • Deneb frees the Seal-eater despite his fear (10) • Vega stays calm in the sea shake (13) and orders the dive (14) • Vega takes responsibility at Land's End (15)
Helping others despite differencesDeneb helps a Seal-eater his family distrusts (10) • the Seal-eater guides Deneb to deep water (12) • porpoises warn everyone, and Deneb understands them (12) • humans in the orange boat cut the line (10) • Vega greets the longboat riders as family (11)
Family / kinshipVega lays Capella with the uncles (8) • Rigel sends Deneb to bring Vega home (9) • Vega calls for Deneb through the chaos (13) • she feels guilty for leaving the family and responsible for Deneb (15)
Grief and anger → compassionVega's rage at humans, then she sees a pregnant woman and child (8) • she wonders whether human poisons hurt human babies too (8)
Humans and natureBlood Cove captures (8) • crab-trap line (10) • longboat riders live in peace with whales (11) • the collapsing bridge and overturned boats (11–14) • poisoned water (15)
Leadership / growing upVega uses memory and Greatmother's teaching to navigate (13) • she saves Deneb and the Seal-eater with the dive (14) • she makes the hard decision at Land's End (15) • Deneb acts alone for the first time (9–10)

Comparing Vega and Deneb's bravery

VegaDeneb
Type of braveryEmotional, thoughtful, responsiblePhysical, impulsive, from the heart
Key momentsFaces grief at Blood Cove; stays calm in the sea shake; orders the dive; takes charge of her brotherLeaves the pod alone; frees the Seal-eater; follows the Seal-eater through the sea shake
What drives itLove for Capella and duty as a wayfinderWanting to be a hero like Uncle Rigel; love for Vega
SimilarityBoth are brave for their family, and both act despite being frightened and young.

📽️ Revision slideshow: The Tyger

The Tyger – William Blake (1794)

Tyger Tyger, burning bright,
In the forests of the night;
What immortal hand or eye,
Could frame thy fearful symmetry?

In what distant deeps or skies,
Burnt the fire of thine eyes?
On what wings dare he aspire?
What the hand, dare seize the fire?

And what shoulder, & what art,
Could twist the sinews of thy heart?
And when thy heart began to beat,
What dread hand? & what dread feet?

What the hammer? what the chain,
In what furnace was thy brain?
What the anvil? what dread grasp,
Dare its deadly terrors clasp!

When the stars threw down their spears
And water'd heaven with their tears:
Did he smile his work to see?
Did he who made the Lamb make thee?

Tyger Tyger burning bright,
In the forests of the night:
What immortal hand or eye,
Dare frame thy fearful symmetry?

Background: The poem comes from Blake's Songs of Experience. It is a partner to "The Lamb" in Songs of Innocence, which shows a gentle, innocent creation. "The Tyger" shows the frightening, powerful side of creation.

Glossary: frame = make, shape; symmetry = perfectly balanced form; deeps = depths of the sea; aspire = rise up; sinews = tendons, muscles; anvil = iron block a blacksmith hammers metal on; immortal = living forever (a god).

Stanza-by-stanza meaning

StanzaMeaningKey technique
1The speaker addresses the tiger, glowing like fire in the dark forest, and asks what god could have made something so beautifully and frighteningly balanced.Apostrophe (speaking to the tiger), repetition "Tyger Tyger", fire imagery "burning bright", contrast of light and dark, and the contrast inside "fearful symmetry"
2Where did the fire in its eyes come from: the depths of the sea or the sky? What creator dared to fly up and seize that fire?Rhetorical questions; myth-like image of a daring creator (like Prometheus stealing fire)
3What strength and skill twisted the tiger's heart muscles? When its heart started beating, what terrible hands and feet did the creator have?Body imagery, the word "dread" repeated, broken questions that sound breathless
4The creator is imagined as a blacksmith with hammer, chain, furnace and anvil, daring to grip the tiger's deadly brain.Extended metaphor of a forge; short, hammering questions; harsh sounds
5When the stars gave up their weapons and cried, did the creator smile at what he made? Could the same god who made the gentle lamb make the tiger?The central question: contrast between Lamb (innocence) and Tyger (experience / danger)
6The first stanza repeated, but "Could frame" becomes "Dare frame".Circular structure; the change from could (ability) to dare (courage) makes making the tiger seem even more dangerous

Form, themes and key quotations

  • Form: 6 quatrains (4-line stanzas) in rhyming couplets (AABB). Strong, regular beat (mostly 7 syllables, stressed-unstressed, like a drumbeat or a hammer).
  • Questions: the poem contains around 13–14 questions and no answers. This shows wonder, confusion and awe.
  • Themes: the power and mystery of creation; good and evil; beauty and danger existing together; innocence vs experience; faith and doubt.
  • Tone: awed, amazed, fearful, questioning.
QuotationWhat to say about it
"burning bright"The tiger's stripes and eyes blaze like fire in the dark. It suggests energy, beauty and danger at once.
"fearful symmetry"An almost contradictory pair: symmetry is beautiful and ordered, but "fearful" makes it terrifying. The tiger is perfect and deadly.
"What the hammer? what the chain"Blacksmith metaphor: the tiger was forged with strength and heat, not gently. Short questions sound like hammer blows.
"Did he who made the Lamb make thee?"The key question: how can one creator make both gentleness and violence?
"Dare frame"Changed from "Could": making the tiger needed courage. The creator is bold, or even reckless.
📽️ Revision slideshow: The Eagle

The Eagle – Alfred, Lord Tennyson (1851)

He clasps the crag with crooked hands;
Close to the sun in lonely lands,
Ring'd with the azure world, he stands.

The wrinkled sea beneath him crawls;
He watches from his mountain walls,
And like a thunderbolt he falls.

Glossary: clasps = grips tightly; crag = a steep, rough rock face; crooked = bent, curved (his talons); ring'd = surrounded; azure = bright sky-blue; thunderbolt = a flash of lightning with thunder.

Line-by-line

LineMeaningTechnique & effect
"He clasps the crag with crooked hands"The eagle grips the rock with its curved talons.Alliteration of hard "c/k" sounds (clasps, crag, crooked) sounds harsh and strong, like his grip. Personification: "hands" and "he" make him seem human, almost like a king.
"Close to the sun in lonely lands"He is very high up, in a remote place.Hyperbole: "close to the sun" exaggerates his height. Alliteration "lonely lands". He is powerful but isolated.
"Ring'd with the azure world, he stands."He is surrounded by blue sky.Imagery: the sky forms a ring or crown around him. "He stands" is a short, proud ending to the stanza: calm, still, in control.
"The wrinkled sea beneath him crawls"From so high, the sea's waves look like wrinkles, and they seem to move slowly.Personification and perspective: the mighty sea looks old, small and weak ("crawls") compared to the eagle.
"He watches from his mountain walls"He keeps watch from the cliffs."his mountain walls" sounds like a castle; the eagle is like a king or guard surveying his kingdom (or a hunter looking for prey).
"And like a thunderbolt he falls."He dives suddenly at great speed (probably to catch prey).Simile: speed, power, danger and suddenness. The poem ends with dramatic action after all the stillness.

Form and themes

  • Form: two tercets (3-line stanzas), rhyme scheme AAA BBB (hands/lands/stands; crawls/walls/falls). Regular iambic tetrameter (8 syllables, da-DUM ×4), which feels controlled and steady, like the eagle.
  • Structure: stanza 1 is stillness (he stands); stanza 2 moves from watching to sudden action (he falls). The final word "falls" is the climax.
  • Themes: power and majesty of nature; isolation; the hunter; perspective (how things look from above).
  • Tone: admiring, awe-struck, calm, then dramatic.

Comparing the two poems

The TygerThe Eagle
Animal shown asBeautiful but terrifying; a mysteryMajestic, kingly, powerful, lonely
SpeakerSpeaks directly to the tiger ("thy"), full of questionsCalm observer describing "he"
Structure6 quatrains, AABB couplets, circular (first stanza repeated)2 tercets, AAA BBB, moves from stillness to action
Key techniquesRhetorical questions, fire and forge imagery, repetitionAlliteration, personification, simile, perspective
Big ideaWho could create such a dangerous, beautiful thing?The eagle rules its high, lonely world and strikes with sudden power
SimilarityBoth make a wild creature seem powerful and awe-inspiring through vivid imagery and strong sound patterns.
📝 Practice sheet: 15 questions, no time limit

Literary devices glossary

DeviceMeaningExample
SimileComparison using like or as"like a thunderbolt he falls"
MetaphorSays something is something elseThe classroom was a zoo.
PersonificationGiving human qualities to non-human things"The wrinkled sea … crawls"
AlliterationRepeated consonant sounds at the start of nearby words"clasps the crag with crooked hands"
AssonanceRepeated vowel sounds"Tyger Tyger, burning bright" (the long "i")
OnomatopoeiaWords that sound like their meaningbuzz, crash, sizzle
ImageryLanguage that creates pictures through the senses"burning bright / In the forests of the night"
Rhetorical questionA question asked for effect, not for an answer"Did he who made the Lamb make thee?"
RepetitionRepeating words or lines for emphasis"Tyger Tyger"; "what dread…"
HyperboleExtreme exaggeration"Close to the sun"
Oxymoron / contrastOpposite ideas placed together"fearful symmetry"
ApostropheSpeaking directly to something that can't answer"Tyger Tyger…" (talking to the tiger)
SymbolismAn object standing for an ideaThe Lamb = innocence; the Tyger = power / danger
Rhyme schemeThe pattern of rhymes, shown with lettersThe Eagle: AAA BBB; The Tyger: AABB
StanzaA group of lines (a "verse paragraph")Couplet (2), tercet (3), quatrain (4)
EnjambmentA sentence running over the end of a line without punctuation"What immortal hand or eye / Could frame…"
Tone / moodThe writer's attitude / the feeling created in the readerAwed, fearful, admiring, calm
